text.p: Franco-Italian food giant Eridania Beghin-Say on Friday predicted stable to slightly higher operating profit this year after reporting a 6.2 percent decline in 1996 earnings.
Cheaper raw farm material prices are expected to help 1997 earnings, but difficulties still plague starch in the United States and sugar in Italy.
"I see operating profit stable, possibly slightly higher," chairman Stefano Meloni told reporters after a news conference on the company's 1996 earnings.
Meloni also predicted turnover might increase this year at the same rate as in 1996 when it grew 8.2 percent to 54.98 billion francs ($9.8 billion).
Eridania announced late on Thursday that net profit grew 8.8 percent to 1.66 billion francs, mostly the result of lower financial costs and extraordinary charges and due to a stable tax rate.
But operating income fell to 3.752 billion francs from 4.001 billion, prompting Eridania to hold its net dividend at 33 francs per share.

In 1996 sugar and animal nutrition managed to improve operating margins while consumer goods just maintained margins. Higher grain and oilseeds prices, the result of poor 1995 harvests, squeezed the profits of the starch unit in the United States and of the crushings and refining division.
Meloni said that 1997 prospects looked good for starch in Europe, animal feed and consumer goods and mixed for crushings and refining.
The outlook for sugar in France and Hungary was good but a poor 1996/97 crop in Italy would still weigh on the group's performance in 1997, he said.
Sugar production in Italy fell sharply last year on the back of a 20 percent fall in beet sowings. The group produced 741,000 tonnes of sugar in Italy in 1996 against 770,000 tonnne in 1995.
Eridania hopes to increase sugar production in Italy to over 800,000 tonnes for the 1997/98 campaign, Meloni said.
In 1996 margins recovered in the starch and derivatives business in Europe as Eridania managed to pass on to customers rises in raw material prices.
But overcapacity plaguing the U.S. high fructose corn syrup market, did limit the bargaining power of starch producers in price negotiations with large soft drink companies.
U.S. starch producers faced a 29 percent rise in maize prices and a six percent fall in their selling prices in 1996.
Meloni said that he did not expect a significant improvement in the U.S. starch sector in 1997 although he hoped Cerestar USA would break even after posting a loss in 1996.
"Volumes are on the rise but once again soft drink companies have taken advantage of a situation of overcapacity," he said.
Meloni was referring to supply contracts negotiated in early 1997 with U.S. soft drink companies.
In consumer goods the Spanish olive oil situation should return to normal in 1997 on the back of a good olive crop, he said.
A poor 1995/96 crop pushed olive oil prices up in Spain, bringing sales volume down by 28 percent in 1996.
But the consumer goods unit Medeol managed to maintain margins, as higher sales of vegetable oil and spices helped offset falling olive oil sales.
